title: Permissions in an analytics tool
excerpt: Say which scope an operator is seeing, and why a row or an export is missing. A total that hides its parts will look wrong even when the rule is correct.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it, marking what each role is allowed to open.
caption: The sketch shows the boundary before the chart does. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a partial scope be shown?
faqs.answer: Say the scope next to the number, every time it is narrower than the company. If some rows are hidden, show a remainder line so the visible parts still add up. A total that does not match its rows will be distrusted, even when the hiding was intentional.

faqs.question: Should exports follow the on-screen permission?
faqs.answer: Yes. A CSV should contain only the rows and columns this role can see, and it should say if a column was left out. A shared link or a Monday email should use that same scope. An embed that keeps an owner's view on a public page is a leak.

faqs.question: Who should be allowed to change a metric definition?
faqs.answer: Let analysts draft and a named owner publish. The homepage should keep the published sentence until that publish happens. Anyone who can silently redefine the number can destroy the only asset the first screen has.

markdown:
Sound analytics tool permissions ux shows an operator what they can see, and why a number, a row, or an export is unavailable. Hiding the control and hoping they will not notice makes a correct total look like a bug.

The W3C's WCAG overview sorts its guidelines into perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A locked metric still has to be perceivable as locked, and the reason has to be understandable. A dashboard that simply omits half the business fails that test.

## Start from the decision, not the matrix

Write the decisions each role is allowed to make, in a sentence. Then decide which figures those decisions require. A regional lead needs their region's revenue and the customers inside it. A finance partner needs the company total and the export. A support lead needs volume and the queue, not margin. An investor update might need a total with no names attached.

If you begin from a grid of checkboxes, you will ship combinations nobody can explain. If you begin from the sentence, the screen can repeat it. "You are seeing the EU shop, because that is your scope." The sentence belongs on the first screen, near the number, every time the scope is narrower than the company.

Roles worth naming out loud:

- Owner: every source, every customer, billing for the tool itself.
- Analyst: build and save views, no access to the tool's invoice.
- Operator: the pinned number and the rows for their scope.
- Guest: a single shared view, no drill-down to personal data.

Add a role when a person is blocked every week. Do not add one because the matrix had an empty column.

## Totals that still add up

The hardest case is a person who may see a total and may not see every part. If you hide the other regions, the visible rows will not sum to the headline, and the operator will distrust both. Prefer a visible remainder. "Other regions, $18,400. Names are hidden for your role." The math works. The boundary is stated. They can do their job without collecting other people's customers.

Do the same for cost, margin, and payroll-shaped numbers. If this role should not see margin, do not include margin in a tooltip on a bar they can hover. Tooltips are still disclosure. If the chart cannot be drawn without the secret, give them a different chart, and say the simpler reason. "This view shows revenue. Margin is limited to finance."

Exports follow the screen, not a wider door. A CSV that contains the rows they cannot see is a broken permission with a download icon. Generate the file from the same scope as the page. If the export is smaller because a column is restricted, say which column was left out. A silent narrower file will be treated as a bug by the person who reconciles it.

## Shared views and private notes

A saved view is a bundle of filters and a name. Say who can open it. "Private to you," "anyone in the EU role," or "anyone with the link." A link that bypasses the role is not a convenience. It is a second permissions system you will forget to audit. If a link exists, it should grant only what the sender could already see, and it should expire, with a page that says it expired.

Comments on a chart, targets, and the note "ignore 4 April, tracking was down" are part of the number's meaning. Decide who can write them and who can read them. A target the operator cannot see will make their comparison look arbitrary. A note about an incident that names a customer does not belong on a guest view. Put the audience on the note, the way you would on a support reply.

Do not let a shared view become a way to request access by osmosis. If someone opens a link above their role, show the view's title and the reason they cannot see the figures. "This is the finance weekly. Your role can see the EU shop home." Offer a path to ask the owner if asking is real. A 403 with no noun is a dead end.

## Sources, segments, and who may connect them

Connecting a new source changes what the company can know. That action belongs to a small set of people, and the screen should say so before a curious operator hunts for it. "Only owners connect billing. You can use the figures once they are connected." Hiding the item in a menu they can still reach, then failing on save, wastes the afternoon.

Segments and definitions are permissions too. If anyone can redefine "active account" and change the homepage number, you do not have a trusted figure. Let analysts draft a definition. Let a named owner publish it. Show the published sentence on the chart. A draft that only the author sees cannot quietly rewrite Monday.

Row-level rules should be described in the cabinet and repeated on the page. "Customers are limited to accounts you own." Test it with a person who owns nothing, a person who owns one account, and a person who owns two. The empty state for the first is "no accounts are assigned to you," not a chart at zero that looks like a dead business. Zero and none are different facts. The copy has to keep them apart.

## When someone leaves

Remove the seat, and decide what happens to their private views, scheduled emails, and shared links. Private views can be deleted or handed to a manager. Scheduled emails must stop or be reassigned on purpose, because a report that keeps landing in a leaver's inbox, or worse, keeps sending from a token they still have, is a permissions failure with a calendar invite.

Review tokens the way you review seats. A personal access token is a role that does not appear in the team list. Say, in settings, which tokens exist and what scope they have, in words an owner can read. "Warehouse read, created by Sam in March." Revoking a seat should not leave the token behind, unless you have a sentence that explains why an integration is the exception.

The first screen should update immediately after a scope change. If a regional lead is moved from EU to US, the next load shows the US number and says so. A cached EU figure with no label is a stale permission, and it will be copied into a deck before the cache expires.

## Scheduled mail and embedded numbers

A Monday email is a permission that walks out of the building. It should contain only what the recipient can see inside the tool, including the remainder line if their scope is partial. If a founder forwards that mail, you cannot stop the forward. You can stop the mail from being the first time a regional lead sees another region's customers. Generate it from the same query as the screen they load.

Embeds on a board page or an intranet follow the same rule, and they rot more quietly. An embed created by an owner may keep the owner's scope long after the page is shown to the whole company. Say, on the embed setting, whose scope it uses. "Shows the company total, with no customer names." If it uses the viewer's scope, say that too, and accept that a logged-out frame cannot show a personal number. A logged-out frame that still shows the owner's book is a leak with a chart in it.

Review these on a calendar. Who receives the Monday note. What an embed showed last week. Whether a leaver is still on either list. The cabinet can hold the controls. The first screen should still wear the scope sentence, so a person who never opens settings is not surprised by a number they were never meant to have, or denied a number they were.

## Make the boundary look intentional

Design the locked states with the open ones. In Figma, every chart that can be restricted needs a version with the remainder line, a version with the role sentence, and a version for the person who should not be here at all. The build, in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, should enforce the same rule on the query and on the render. Prisma and PostgreSQL can hold the seat, the scope, and the saved view so the sentence on the page is generated from the rule, not typed ad hoc per chart.

People who cannot see the row they expected will search for the customer, the metric, or the view by name. [Search inside an analytics tool](/blog/search-inside-an-analytics-tool) is the next piece, because search has to respect the same scope, and it has to offer a way back when the name they typed is real but not theirs to open.

Hanabi's work on product interfaces starts from what a role is allowed to finish. See [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) if your dashboards disagree with each other depending on who is logged in. Bring the sentence for each role. The screens should be able to repeat it.
